metadata.title: Complex Cobordism vs Representing Formal Group Laws

extraction_notes.note: One sentence both states the Borel-Serre result (external) and derives the paper's equivalence modulo torsion; it cannot be split, so it is one paper claim with Borel-Serre as its assumption.
Two examples exist only as figure captions with xypic diagrams; the caption text is the statement.
Proofs are prose paragraphs preceding the lemma/claim they justify; start and end chosen by reading.

nodes.name: Ravenel's question on infinite loopspace theory and complex cobordism
nodes.statement: We attempt to answer a question of D. C. Ravenel's: ``\textit{Infinite loopspace theorists, where are you?}'', or more prosaically: Can one start from the notion of Ring Spectrum Representing [Formal Group Laws] (the functor) and arrive at Complex Cobordism?
nodes.statement_short: Can complex cobordism be obtained starting from the ring spectrum representing formal group laws?

nodes.name: Milnor's theorem; Landweber-Novikov theorem
nodes.statement: Milnor showed that the cohomology ring $MU$ was {\em naturally} isomorphic to Lazard's ring $\Lambda$, while Landweber \cite{landweber} and Novikov \cite{novikov} show the stronger result that the Hopf algebra $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ {\em naturally} represents Lazard's Hopf algebra.
conclusions: the cohomology ring $MU$ was {\em naturally} isomorphic to Lazard's ring $\Lambda$
the Hopf algebra $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ {\em naturally} represents Lazard's Hopf algebra
nodes.statement_short: $MU^*$ is naturally Lazard's ring and $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ represents Lazard's Hopf algebra.

nodes.name: Notation for complex projective space and its powers
nodes.statement: We write $\mathbb{CP}$ for infinite complex projective space, $\mathbb{CP}_k$ for its usual $2k$-skeleta, and will otherwise (try to) emphasize monoidal structures in superscripts: $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$ is a $k$-fold direct product, $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ a $k$-fold smash, et.c.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{CP}$ is infinite complex projective space, $\mathbb{CP}_k$ its skeleta; $\times k$ / $\wedge k$ superscripts are products / smashes.

nodes.name: Symmetric group, Borel quotient and cofiber notation
nodes.statement: We use $k!$ as the name of the symmetric group on $[k]$ (the von Neumann ordinal, for definiteness), whose cardinality is the usual significance of ``$k!$''; Borel quotient is denoted $/\!/ $ and cofiber is $/$; in particular $*/\!/ G \simeq \mathbf{B} G$.
nodes.statement_short: $k!$ denotes the symmetric group on $[k]$; $/\!/$ is Borel quotient and $/$ is cofiber.

nodes.name: Generalized Thom space (twisted half-smash)
nodes.statement: In any case, our twisted half smashes, or generalized Thom spaces, are denoted and defined as $$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(X,F) \simeq E/X $$ where $X \to E \to X$ is a section/retract with fibers $F\to E \to X$.
nodes.statement_short: The generalized Thom space of a section/retract $X\to E\to X$ with fiber $F$ is the cofiber $E/X$.

nodes.name: Thom space of a group action as cofiber of Borel quotients
nodes.statement: In particular, the Thom space of a group action in the pointed category is a cofiber of Borel quotients: $$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} G, X) \simeq (X/\!/ G) / (*/\!/ G) .$$
conclusions: the Thom space of a group action in the pointed category is a cofiber of Borel quotients

nodes.name: Coherent cube; homotopy (co)limit convention
nodes.statement: In fact what diagrams we use are, almost exclusively, coherent cubes, which are diagrams all of whose cubical facets are ``contractible'', to the extent that makes sense; and whenever we say ``colimit'' or ``cofiber'' or ``fiber'' we mean, exclusively, {\em homotopy}-colimit, {\em homotopy}-(co)fiber, et.c.
differentia: all of whose cubical facets are ``contractible'', to the extent that makes sense
nodes.statement_short: Coherent cubes are diagrams whose cubical facets are contractible; (co)limits and (co)fibers are always homotopical.

nodes.name: Distributivity
nodes.statement: Lastly, within the usual Kelley category of CG[w]Hf spaces, one has Mather's Cube theorems; we call the {\em result} of Mather's theorems (and its finitary corollaries over any colimit) {\em distributivity}, after the obvious arithmetic analogue.
nodes.statement_short: Distributivity names the result of Mather's cube theorems and their finitary corollaries over colimits.

nodes.name: Finitary distributivity as an axiom of unstable homotopy
nodes.statement: Note that its use in homotopy is decades older than Mather's published proofs, underlying at least one classic construction of the Leray-Serre spectral sequence, (see also in particular the works of Tudor Ganea), and we use finitary distributivity as a general {\em axiom} of [unstable] homotopy.

nodes.name: Complex-oriented ring spectra support formal group laws
nodes.statement: That is, given a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ (suitable for Atiyah-Hirzebruch purposes) and a class $g : \Lambda^2(\mathbb{CP})$ extending the fundamental class $\eta: \Lambda^2(\mathbb{S}^2)\sim \Lambda^0(*)\ni 1$, pull-back along tensor product of lines $\otimes: \mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP} \to \mathbb{CP}$ induces a ring homomorphism $\Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}) \to \Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP})$ which (due to the goodness of $g$ and collapsing spectral sequences) gives a formal group law $$ \Lambda^*(\mathbb{S})[x] \to \Lambda^*(\mathbb{S})[x\otimes 1,1\otimes x] .$$
assumptions: given a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ (suitable for Atiyah-Hirzebruch purposes) and a class $g : \Lambda^2(\mathbb{CP})$ extending the fundamental class $\eta: \Lambda^2(\mathbb{S}^2)\sim \Lambda^0(*)\ni 1$
conclusions: pull-back along tensor product of lines $\otimes: \mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP} \to \mathbb{CP}$ induces a ring homomorphism $\Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}) \to \Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP})$ which (due to the goodness of $g$ and collapsing spectral sequences) gives a formal group law
nodes.statement_short: A complex orientation $g$ of a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ yields a formal group law via the tensor product of lines.

nodes.name: Principal tools behind the formal group law of a complex orientation
nodes.statement: It may be worth remarking that the principal tools in the preceding are: the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence collapses for an even-concentrated cohomology theory over an even-concentrated space; and the ordinary cohomology of $\mathbb{CP}$ is the ordinary polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$; this feature it shares with the \textit{homology} of the odd-sphere loopspaces $\Omega \mathbb{S}^{2n+1}$; indeed the Hopf Algebras $H^*(\mathbb{CP})$ and $H_*(\Omega\mathbb{S}^{2n+1})$ are isomorphic, which means it's hard to see (except that $\otimes$ is plainly special) why one should prefer {\em co}homology for FGL purposes. In other words, if this is already too much hypothesis in the direction of the conclusion for Ravenel's intent\dots \textit{H\'elas!}
nodes.statement_short: The FGL construction rests on AHSS collapse and $H^*(\mathbb{CP})=\mathbb{Z}[x]$, a feature shared with $H_*(\Omega\mathbb{S}^{2n+1})$.

nodes.name: Minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum
nodes.statement: {\em Having} chosen to reflect FGLs by complex-oriented ring spectra, one can clearly ask: what is the minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum? And this in turn means: what is the ring spectrum $\Lambda$ {\em generated by} a map $\mathbb{CP} \to \Lambda_2$?
nodes.statement_short: Find the minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum, i.e. the ring spectrum generated by a map $\mathbb{CP}\to\Lambda_2$.

nodes.name: Approximating spaces $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement: Using this model (cf. \cite{mayRings}) it is straightforward that our ring spectrum $\Lambda$ should be approximated by the spaces $$ L_{2k} = \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) $$ with prespectrum maps induced by $$ \mathbb{S}^2 \wedge L_{2k} \to \mathbb{CP} \wedge L_{2k} \to L_{2k+2} $$
nodes.statement_short: $L_{2k}$ is the generalized Thom space $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$, with prespectrum maps via $\mathbb{CP}\wedge L_{2k}\to L_{2k+2}$.

nodes.name: Universality of the $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement: But the reason is simple: the $L_{2k}$ are already universal.
conclusions: the $L_{2k}$ are already universal

nodes.name: Proof of universality of the $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement: More: it is required, for any commutative ring spectrum $E$ and orientation $\mathbb{CP}\to E_2$, that we have {\em ring maps} $\Lambda_k \to E_k$; and ``ring maps'' {\em means} commutativity $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!, \Lambda_l^{\wedge k}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,E_l^{\wedge k}) \ar[d]\\ \Lambda_{kl} \ar[r] & E_{kl} }\end{xy} $$ Thus on the one hand, it is {\em necessary} that $$\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!, E_2^{\wedge k}) \ar[d] \\ L_{2k} \ar[r] & E_{2k} } \end{xy} $$ commutes; and on the other hand, there is {\em exactly} one way for this to happen when the left arrow is an identity.
nodes.statement_short: Ring maps force the square from $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ to commute, uniquely when the left arrow is the identity.

nodes.name: Direct-sum map
nodes.statement: Since direct sum is plainly a useful $E_\infty$ construction on complex vector spaces (this is, after Segal, what makes $\mathbf{B} U$ an infinite loopspace), it is the most natural thing in geometry to consider the maps $$ \bigoplus : \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \to \mathbf{B} U(k).$$
nodes.statement_short: The direct-sum map $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: That is: the Thom space is described as the quotient (cofiber) of a (vector space or disk) bundle by the inclusion of the bundle of spheres (at-infinity or unit spheres); but for homotopy purposes, the important feature is the bundle of spheres itself, which is to say the map $$ E \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$ whose fibers are the unit spheres of the tautological bundle. The usual discussion of disk bundle and sphere-at-infinity acheives the necessary trivial-fibration$\circ$cofibration replacement in any of the classic model-category structures; however, the result of the construction is the (we now don't need to {\em say} ``homotopy'') cofiber. Therefore, for the purposes of homotopy, it is sufficient to identify the type of the map $E\to U(k)$; but this is easy: the unit sphere is the (Borel, or ordinary) quotient $U(k)/\!/ U(k-1)$; the canonical action of $U(k)$ on this has Borel quotient equivalent to $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ and by functoriality of $\mathbf{B}$ the quotient {\em map} is the fiber map $$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$
nodes.statement_short: Thom space is the cofiber of the sphere bundle; the unit sphere bundle of the tautological bundle is $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$.

nodes.name: Thom space $MU(k)$ as cofiber
nodes.statement: $$ MU(k) \simeq \mathbf{B} U(k) / \mathbf{B} U(k-1) $$
also_stated_at: the ordinary Thom spaces $MU(k)$ are the cofibers of the usual maps $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$
conclusions: $$ MU(k) \simeq \mathbf{B} U(k) / \mathbf{B} U(k-1) $$
nodes.statement_short: $MU(k)$ is the cofiber of $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$.

nodes.name: Thom space of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ as cofiber of the direct-sum source
nodes.statement: From the source of the direct-sum map, we have another natural map $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \to \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) $$ which is, like $\mathbf{B} U(k)\to MU(k)$, a cofiber map.
conclusions: which is, like $\mathbf{B} U(k)\to MU(k)$, a cofiber map

nodes.name: Pasting diagram of pushouts for the fat wedge
nodes.statement: There is a pasting diagram of pushouts $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\ \mathbf{B} k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r] & \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!, \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) } \end{xy} $$
conclusions: There is a pasting diagram of pushouts $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\ \mathbf{B} k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r] & \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!, \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) } \end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ arises from $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!$ by pasting pushouts along the fat wedge and $\mathbf{B}k!$.

nodes.name: Fat wedge $W^k\mathbb{CP}$
nodes.statement: Specifically, $W^k \mathbb{CP}$ is the so-called ``fat wedge'', which we shall study more closely in the next sections.

nodes.name: Summary diagram of cofiber sequences
nodes.statement: But to summarize the state of things now, we have the following diagram, of which the verticals are cofiber sequences $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \mathbb{CP}/\!/ k! \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k) \ar[d] \\ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) & MU(k) }\end{xy}$$
nodes.statement_short: Diagram comparing the cofiber sequences ending in $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ and $MU(k)$.

nodes.name: Cube of coordinate planes
nodes.statement: In any category with products, for any pointed object $* \to X$ and any $k:\mathbb{N}$ there is a commuting $k$-cube of coordinate planes: the cube of pullbacks of $k$ inclusions $$ X^{k-1} \to X^k $$ which themselves are the fibers {\em at} $*\to X$ of the $k$ defining structure maps $X^k \to X$.
differentia: the cube of pullbacks of $k$ inclusions $$ X^{k-1} \to X^k $$ which themselves are the fibers {\em at} $*\to X$ of the $k$ defining structure maps $X^k \to X$
nodes.statement_short: For pointed $X$, the $k$-cube of coordinate planes is the cube of pullbacks of the $k$ inclusions $X^{k-1}\to X^k$.

nodes.name: Small coordinate-plane cubes ($k=1,2,3$)
nodes.statement: Small instances of the coordinate planes cube are $$ * \to X \qquad (k=1) $$ $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ {*} \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^{(*,id)} \\ X \ar[r]_{(id,*)} & X^2 } \end{xy} (k=2) $$ $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix@=1.2em{ {*} \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] & & X \ar[dr] \ar[dd]|\hole\\ & X \ar[dd] \ar[rr] & & X^2 \ar[dd] \\ X \ar[rr]|\hole \ar[dr] & & X^2 \ar[dr] \\ & X^2 \ar[rr] & & X^3 }\end{xy} (k=3) $$

nodes.name: Blooms and fat wedges
nodes.statement: Though it is more generality than we need, different truncations of these diagrams (\dots the truncations should have a snappy name; I will call them ``blooms'') have colimits that generalize wedge sums, including, in particular, the ``fat wedge''; for the sake of convenience in notating $W^k X /\!/ k!$, we have chosen to index the fat wedges by the dimension of ambient cube defining them, rather than the degree of their petals.
nodes.statement_short: Blooms are truncations of the coordinate-planes cube whose colimits generalize wedges, e.g. the fat wedge $W^kX$, indexed by cube dimension.

nodes.name: Wedge of three copies as a bloom colimit
nodes.statement: \caption{\small Example: Wedge of three $X$s; the bloom looks like a sparse parsley inflorescence}

nodes.name: Fat wedge $W^3X$ as a bloom colimit
nodes.statement: \caption{\small Example: $W^3 X$; this bloom looks more like a tulip; in both examples, the dotted portions are generated as an initial Kan extension, to the cube, of the (solid-arrow) bloom}

nodes.name: Construction of the lifting square (proof of Lemma 3)
nodes.statement: Our purpose in reminding the reader of this construction (who likely enough knows it already) is to prepare for the construction of the actual lifting, a map $W^k \mathbb{CP}/\!/ k! \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$; since $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is a {\em colimit}, constructing a map out of it is accomplished by constructing a coherent cube, such as $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix@=1.2em{ {*} \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] & & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dr] \ar[dd]|\hole\\ & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dd] \ar[rr] & & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dd] \\ \mathbb{CP} \ar[rr]|\hole \ar[dr] & & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dr] & & \mbox{(Do I exist?)} \\ & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[rr] & & \mathbf{B} U(2) }\end{xy} $$ Now, this in itself is {\em not sufficient} for that we want a map on the Borel quotient $W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/ k!$, of which $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is just one fiber over $* \to \mathbf{B} k!$; and so we shall also have to take care that our constructed cube is suitably equivariant. There isn't much choice about the maps towards the terminal vertex in the wanted diagram: we have direct sum, $\mathbb{CP}^{k-1}\to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$, and anything hugely different is likely to be too forgetful. We have already described the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ as the tautological sphere bundle over $\mathbf{B} U(k)$ $$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$ which is to say that a point of $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ over $V:\mathbf{B} U(k)$ corresponds to {\em a unit vector in $V$}, which also articulates the sense in which the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ is direct sum {\em with $\mathbb{C}$} and not just {\em any line}; in terms of the space $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ as classifier of $k-1$-dimensional complex vector spaces, a unit vector in $V$ corresponds to {\em the orthogonal complement} of that vector; and so a composite $\mathbf{B} U(k-2) \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ further corresponds to {\em an ordered pair} of orthogonal unit vectors in $V$, and classifies the orthogonal complement of their span, et.c. What matters for us is: the action of $k!$ on the relevant cubes {\em permutes these orders}; or, for now passing over the action of $k!$, the possible obstruction to homotopy commutativity in $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) }\end{xy}$$ is that the two routes have chosen orthogonal vectors in $V$, the unambiguous vector space specified by the unambiguous composite $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$. To specify the commutativity of the square, it is sufficient to specify a homotopy in unit vectors between these orthogonal two. Happily, a basis for a complex space induces an inclusion of a real space with a basis, and in a real space with a basis, the positive orthant of the unit sphere does everything we need! Being described in such dimension-agnostic terms, it is also clear how to generalize the argument to other layers of the cube, and commutativity with the already-known maps to $\mathbf{B} U(k)$. And, hopefully, the equivariance of the construction is also sufficiently evident.
nodes.statement_short: Build an equivariant coherent cube out of the fat wedge to $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)$; squares commute via homotopies of unit vectors in the positive orthant.

nodes.name: A map out of the colimit $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is a coherent cube, which must also be equivariant
nodes.statement: Our purpose in reminding the reader of this construction (who likely enough knows it already) is to prepare for the construction of the actual lifting, a map $W^k \mathbb{CP}/\!/ k! \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$; since $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is a {\em colimit}, constructing a map out of it is accomplished by constructing a coherent cube, such as $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix@=1.2em{ {*} \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] & & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dr] \ar[dd]|\hole\\ & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dd] \ar[rr] & & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dd] \\ \mathbb{CP} \ar[rr]|\hole \ar[dr] & & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dr] & & \mbox{(Do I exist?)} \\ & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[rr] & & \mathbf{B} U(2) }\end{xy} $$ Now, this in itself is {\em not sufficient} for that we want a map on the Borel quotient $W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/ k!$, of which $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is just one fiber over $* \to \mathbf{B} k!$; and so we shall also have to take care that our constructed cube is suitably equivariant.
nodes.statement_short: A map out of the colimit $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is a coherent cube, which must also be equivariant

nodes.name: The maps to the terminal vertex must be direct sums
nodes.statement: There isn't much choice about the maps towards the terminal vertex in the wanted diagram: we have direct sum, $\mathbb{CP}^{k-1}\to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$, and anything hugely different is likely to be too forgetful.
nodes.statement_short: The maps to the terminal vertex must be direct sums

nodes.name: Recall: points of $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)$ over $V$ are unit vectors in $V$
nodes.statement: We have already described the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ as the tautological sphere bundle over $\mathbf{B} U(k)$ $$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$ which is to say that a point of $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ over $V:\mathbf{B} U(k)$ corresponds to {\em a unit vector in $V$}, which also articulates the sense in which the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ is direct sum {\em with $\mathbb{C}$} and not just {\em any line}; in terms of the space $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ as classifier of $k-1$-dimensional complex vector spaces, a unit vector in $V$ corresponds to {\em the orthogonal complement} of that vector; and so a composite $\mathbf{B} U(k-2) \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ further corresponds to {\em an ordered pair} of orthogonal unit vectors in $V$, and classifies the orthogonal complement of their span, et.c.
nodes.statement_short: Recall: points of $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)$ over $V$ are unit vectors in $V$

nodes.name: Identify the obstruction: the two routes choose orthogonal unit vectors
nodes.statement: What matters for us is: the action of $k!$ on the relevant cubes {\em permutes these orders}; or, for now passing over the action of $k!$, the possible obstruction to homotopy commutativity in $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) }\end{xy}$$ is that the two routes have chosen orthogonal vectors in $V$, the unambiguous vector space specified by the unambiguous composite $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to giving a homotopy between orthogonal unit vectors
nodes.statement: To specify the commutativity of the square, it is sufficient to specify a homotopy in unit vectors between these orthogonal two.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to giving a homotopy between orthogonal unit vectors

nodes.name: Construct the homotopy in the positive orthant of the real unit sphere
nodes.statement: Happily, a basis for a complex space induces an inclusion of a real space with a basis, and in a real space with a basis, the positive orthant of the unit sphere does everything we need!
nodes.statement_short: Construct the homotopy in the positive orthant of the real unit sphere

nodes.name: Generalize to all layers of the cube, equivariantly
nodes.statement: Being described in such dimension-agnostic terms, it is also clear how to generalize the argument to other layers of the cube, and commutativity with the already-known maps to $\mathbf{B} U(k)$. And, hopefully, the equivariance of the construction is also sufficiently evident.
nodes.statement_short: Generalize to all layers of the cube, equivariantly

nodes.name: Lifting square and map to $MU(k)$
nodes.statement: We therefore claim a commutative square $$ \xymatrix{W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r]\ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1)\ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k)} $$ and hence a map $$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \to MU(k) .$$
conclusions: a commutative square $$ \xymatrix{W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r]\ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1)\ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k)} $$
a map $$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \to MU(k) .$$
nodes.statement_short: The fat wedge quotient lifts to $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)$ over the direct-sum map, giving a map $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})\to MU(k)$.
nodes.label: liftingsquare

nodes.name: Fiber sequence for the fat wedge inclusion
nodes.statement: The fiber of including a fat wedge in a product $W^k X \to X^k$, (and therefore the fiber of the map $W^k \mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k!$ as well) is, by Distributivity, the $k$-fold self-join of the loopspace $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$; and so we have the small surprise: a fiber sequence $$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! $$
conclusions: a fiber sequence $$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! $$
nodes.statement_short: The fiber of $W^kX\to X^k$ is the join $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$, giving a fiber sequence $\mathbb{S}^{2k-1}\to W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/k!\to\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!$.

nodes.name: The lifting square is a pullback
nodes.statement: In fact, we will argue that the square we already constructed by an interpolation argument (resulting in Lemma \ref{liftingsquare}), is a pullback.
conclusions: is a pullback

nodes.name: Proof that the lifting square is a pullback
nodes.statement: We will work on the $k!$-space rather than the borel quotient, for now, but the equivariance of the argument should be clear. To keep a handle on things, we'll start by naming the pullback itself $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \ar[r]_\oplus & \mathbf{B} U(k) }\end{xy} $$ To begin with, note once more that a point of $R_k$ over $x : \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} $ is specified by a unit vector {\em in} $\oplus x$. Note furthermore that $x$ {\em is} (or might as well be) a {\em split} complex vector space: it comes with a prefered list of independent lines; this in turn gives the unit sphere in $\oplus x$, {\em canonically}, the structure of a join of (unpointed) circles: $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ {\underset{j}{\bigstar}\,\mathbb{S}(x_j)} \ar[r] \ar[d] & R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r]_{(x_j|j=1\dots k)} & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k) }\end{xy}$$ Moreover, this join itself is the colimit of the penultimate bloom within the product cube of the $k$ trivial maps $\mathbb{S}(x_j) \to *$. Integrating this fiberwise decomposition over the base space $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$, the pullback $R_k$ is similarly the colimit of the bloom of various maps of total spaces; but this bloom lives in a cube again seen (with a little care) to be equivalently the cube of coordinate planes in $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$. Consequently, $$ R_k \simeq W^k \mathbb{CP} .$$
nodes.statement_short: Name the pullback $R_k$; fiberwise the unit sphere of $\oplus x$ is a join of circles, a bloom colimit, so $R_k\simeq W^k\mathbb{CP}$.

nodes.name: Work on the $k!$-space and name the pullback $R_k$
nodes.statement: We will work on the $k!$-space rather than the borel quotient, for now, but the equivariance of the argument should be clear. To keep a handle on things, we'll start by naming the pullback itself $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \ar[r]_\oplus & \mathbf{B} U(k) }\end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: Work on the $k!$-space and name the pullback $R_k$

nodes.name: Points of $R_k$ over $x$ are unit vectors in $\oplus x$
nodes.statement: To begin with, note once more that a point of $R_k$ over $x : \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} $ is specified by a unit vector {\em in} $\oplus x$.
nodes.statement_short: Points of $R_k$ over $x$ are unit vectors in $\oplus x$

nodes.name: The unit sphere in $\oplus x$ is canonically a join of circles, the colimit of the penultimate bloom
nodes.statement: Note furthermore that $x$ {\em is} (or might as well be) a {\em split} complex vector space: it comes with a prefered list of independent lines; this in turn gives the unit sphere in $\oplus x$, {\em canonically}, the structure of a join of (unpointed) circles: $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ {\underset{j}{\bigstar}\,\mathbb{S}(x_j)} \ar[r] \ar[d] & R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r]_{(x_j|j=1\dots k)} & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k) }\end{xy}$$ Moreover, this join itself is the colimit of the penultimate bloom within the product cube of the $k$ trivial maps $\mathbb{S}(x_j) \to *$.
nodes.statement_short: The unit sphere in $\oplus x$ is canonically a join of circles, the colimit of the penultimate bloom

nodes.name: Globalize: $R_k$ is a bloom colimit in the coordinate-planes cube
nodes.statement: Integrating this fiberwise decomposition over the base space $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$, the pullback $R_k$ is similarly the colimit of the bloom of various maps of total spaces; but this bloom lives in a cube again seen (with a little care) to be equivalently the cube of coordinate planes in $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Globalize: $R_k$ is a bloom colimit in the coordinate-planes cube

nodes.name: Conclude $R_k\simeq W^k\mathbb{CP}$
nodes.statement: Consequently, $$ R_k \simeq W^k \mathbb{CP} .$$
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $R_k\simeq W^k\mathbb{CP}$

nodes.name: Cofiber $Y_k$ and pushout $P_k$
nodes.statement: The cofiber --- let us call it $Y_k$ --- is, of course, the Total Cofiber of a pullback square, which means it is also the cofiber of the comparison map between the base $\mathbf{B} U(k)$ and the pushout of the pullback structure maps: $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \ar@/^/[ddr] \\ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar@/_/[drr] & P_k \ar[dr] \\ & & \mathbf{B} U(k) }\end{xy} $$ $$ Y_k \simeq \mathbf{B} U(k) / P_k \simeq MU(k) / \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} ) $$
nodes.statement_short: $Y_k$ is the cofiber of $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})\to MU(k)$, equivalently $\mathbf{B}U(k)/P_k$ with $P_k$ the pushout.

nodes.name: Fibers presenting $Y_k$ are joins
nodes.statement: Distributivity now tells us that the {\em fibers} of the new map presenting $Y_k$ are the join of the vertical and horizontal fibers: $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \times F_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \ar[d] \ar@/^/[ddr] \\ F_k \ar[r] \ar@/_/[drr] & \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \star F_k \ar[dr] \\ & & {*} & \rlap{$\mbox{fibers over }\mathbf{B} U(k)$} } \end{xy} $$
conclusions: the {\em fibers} of the new map presenting $Y_k$ are the join of the vertical and horizontal fibers
nodes.statement_short: By distributivity, fibers of $P_k\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$ are $\mathbb{S}^{2k-1}\star F_k$.

nodes.name: The group $G$ (normalizer of the maximal torus)
nodes.statement: As plainly as possible, there are a split extension of groups $$ 1\to \mathbb{T}^k \to G \to k!\to 1 $$ and various (conjugate) inclusions $$ \mathbb{T}^k \to G \to U(k) $$ realizing a maximal torus in $U(k)$. Concretely, one may take $G$ generated by the diagonal matrices and the permutation matrices.
nodes.statement_short: $G$ is the split extension of $k!$ by $\mathbb{T}^k$, generated by diagonal and permutation matrices in $U(k)$.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!$ classifies $G$; identification of $F_k$
nodes.statement: Continuing, $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \simeq \mathbf{B} G $$ $$ F_k \simeq U(k) /\!/ G \simeq (U(k) /\!/ \mathbb{T}^k)/\!/ k! $$
conclusions: $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \simeq \mathbf{B} G $$
$$ F_k \simeq U(k) /\!/ G \simeq (U(k) /\!/ \mathbb{T}^k)/\!/ k! $$

nodes.name: $\mathbb{S}^{2k-1}\star F_k$ is not highly connected
nodes.statement: When I began working towards this note, I wanted to tell you how very-connected $\mathbb{S}^{2k-1}\star F_k$ must be, but, alas, it is not!
conclusions: it is not!

nodes.name: Flag manifolds are simply connected, so $\pi_1F_k\simeq k!$
nodes.statement: There is a simple induction argument that each (complex) flag manifold $V_k = U(k)/\!/ \mathbb{T}^k$ is simply connected: there are fiber sequences $$ V_k \to V_{k+1} \to \mathbb{CP}_k $$ and the base case $V_2 \simeq \mathbb{CP}_1$; this means that $\pi_1 F_k \simeq k!$, so that $\pi_2 \Sigma F_k \simeq C_2 = \mathrm{ab}(k!) $.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on fiber sequences $V_k\to V_{k+1}\to\mathbb{CP}_k$ shows flag manifolds simply connected, so $\pi_1F_k\simeq k!$.

nodes.name: Rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement: In particular, $$ H^*(L_{2k}; \mathbb{Q}) \simeq (H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k};\mathbb{Q}))^{k!} $$ That is, the rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$ is the $k!$-invariants of the [already-torsion-free] homology of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ (because for finite $G$, all extensions of finitely-generated $\mathbb{Q}[G]$-modules are split).
conclusions: $$ H^*(L_{2k}; \mathbb{Q}) \simeq (H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k};\mathbb{Q}))^{k!} $$
nodes.statement_short: $H^*(L_{2k};\mathbb{Q})$ is the $k!$-invariants of $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k};\mathbb{Q})$.

nodes.name: $L_{2k}\to MU(k)$ is an equivalence modulo torsion
nodes.statement: A result that should be well-known due to Borel+Serre \cite{borSer} that in ordinary cohomology, $H^*(\mathbf{B} U(k),\mathbb{Z}) \to H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\times k};\mathbb{Z})$ is {\em exactly} the inclusion of the $k!$-invariants; it will follow from this, since we have an explicit-enough factorization of the maps $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} \to \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \to MU(k), $$ and from the multiplicative underpinning of the Thom isomorphism, that our map $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence {\em modulo torsion}.
assumptions: in ordinary cohomology, $H^*(\mathbf{B} U(k),\mathbb{Z}) \to H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\times k};\mathbb{Z})$ is {\em exactly} the inclusion of the $k!$-invariants
conclusions: our map $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence {\em modulo torsion}
nodes.statement_short: Using Borel-Serre's description of $H^*(\mathbf{B}U(k))$ as $k!$-invariants, $L_{2k}\to MU(k)$ is a rational equivalence.

nodes.name: Complex cobordism is the initial torsion-free complex-orientable ring spectrum
nodes.statement: We can therefore, perhaps, give Ravenel the more concrete answer: Complex Cobordism is the initial {\em torsion-free} complex-orientable ring spectrum.
conclusions: Complex Cobordism is the initial {\em torsion-free} complex-orientable ring spectrum

nodes.name: Cartan-Leray spectral sequence
nodes.statement: The Cartan-Leray spectral sequence tells us $$ H_p( k! ; H_q(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k},\mathbb{F})) \Rightarrow H_{p+q} (\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k!) $$ while the cofiber map trivializes a direct summand $H_*(k!)\hookrightarrow H_*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k!)$, the image of the retract $\mathbf{B} k!$ of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k!$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $$ H_p( k! ; H_q(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k},\mathbb{F})) \Rightarrow H_{p+q} (\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/  k!) $$
nodes.statement_short: Cartan-Leray spectral sequence for the Borel quotient by $k!$; the cofiber map kills the summand $H_*(k!)$.

nodes.name: Homology of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ as $k!$-representation
nodes.statement: The $H_*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ happen to be sums of (possibly trivial) tensor products of the tautological representation; the rational case of this sequence (and sufficient evidence of its collapse) has already been used in \mbox{section \ref{rescue}}.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum

nodes.name: Betley's homological stability
nodes.statement: For any functor $T \in Ab^\Gamma$ of finite degree $d$, the natural map $$H_i( (n-1)! ; T ([n-1])) \to H_i( n! ; T([n])) $$ is an isomorphism provided $2i + d < n$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: the natural map $$H_i( (n-1)! ; T ([n-1])) \to H_i( n! ; T([n])) $$ is an isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Twisted homology of symmetric groups with coefficients in a finite-degree $\Gamma$-module stabilizes for $2i+d<n$.
nodes.label: betstable

nodes.name: The category $\Gamma$ and degree of a $\Gamma$-module
nodes.statement: Here, $\Gamma$ is the category of {\em partial} maps of finite sets; the {\em degree} of such an Abelian functor is defined there in terms of the joint kernels of forgetting: a functor $T$ is of degree at-most $d$ whenever, for all $d$-part partitions $X = \coprod_j X_j$, the natural maps $$ T(X) \to \bigoplus_i T(\coprod_{j\neq i} X_j) $$ are all injective.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma$ is partial maps of finite sets; $T$ has degree $\le d$ if $T(X)\to\bigoplus_i T(\coprod_{j\ne i}X_j)$ is injective for $d$-part partitions.

nodes.name: Cell-counting argument for Lemma 5
nodes.statement: For stable-homotopy purposes, we are interested in the homology groups $H_{2k+j}(\rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ for $j\lesssim J$; that is, we are concerned only with the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash. Particularly, the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ consists of $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells (apart from the basepoint). More: in $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$, nontrivial cells are products of $k$ nontrivial cells in $\mathbb{CP}$, of even dimensions, at least $2$; if their total dimension is not more than $2k+2J$, then at most $J$ of the factors are of dimension {\em greater} than $2$; that is, if $k > J$, all the cells in the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ are contained in an image of $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge l} \wedge \mathbb{S}^2 \wedge \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k-l-1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} $$ and an easy amplification of this argument to $J+1$ smash factors leads us to the conclusion:
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Cells of the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ have at most $J$ factors above dimension 2, so the homology has degree at most $J$.

nodes.name: Restrict to the $2k+2J$-skeleton
nodes.statement: For stable-homotopy purposes, we are interested in the homology groups $H_{2k+j}(\rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ for $j\lesssim J$; that is, we are concerned only with the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the $2k+2J$-skeleton

nodes.name: Count the cells of the skeleton
nodes.statement: Particularly, the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ consists of $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells (apart from the basepoint).
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Count the cells of the skeleton

nodes.name: Cells lie in images of smash factors with an $\mathbb{S}^2$; amplify to $J+1$ factors
nodes.statement: More: in $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$, nontrivial cells are products of $k$ nontrivial cells in $\mathbb{CP}$, of even dimensions, at least $2$; if their total dimension is not more than $2k+2J$, then at most $J$ of the factors are of dimension {\em greater} than $2$; that is, if $k > J$, all the cells in the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ are contained in an image of $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge l} \wedge \mathbb{S}^2 \wedge \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k-l-1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} $$ and an easy amplification of this argument to $J+1$ smash factors leads us to the conclusion:

nodes.statement_short: Cells lie in images of smash factors with an $\mathbb{S}^2$; amplify to $J+1$ factors

nodes.name: Finite degree of the homology of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$
nodes.statement: $H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$, for $j < 2J$, extends along $[k] : \Gamma$ as a functor of degree at most $J$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$, for $j < 2J$, extends along $[k] : \Gamma$ as a functor of degree at most $J$

nodes.name: Stabilization of twisted homology of $k!$
nodes.statement: Consequently $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ stabilizes for $2 p + J \leq k$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ stabilizes for $2 p + J \leq k$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: This establishes that the pages $E^2_{*,*}$ of the Cartan-Leray spectral sequences are stable in the sense necessary for $L_{2k}$ to approximate a finite-type spectrum; concluding that $L_{2k}$ themselves stabilize reduces to arguing that the prespectrum maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to \mathbb{CP}\wedge L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ {\em realize} the morphisms shown in \mbox{Lemma \ref{betstable}} to become isomorphisms; but this already follows from the usual calculation of $H_i(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Stable $E^2$ pages of Cartan-Leray plus the prespectrum maps realizing Betley's isomorphisms make $L_{2k}$ stabilize.

nodes.name: $L_*$ presents the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum
nodes.statement: The spaces $L_{2k}$ with the maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ approximate a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$; this is the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: The spaces $L_{2k}$ with the maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ approximate a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$
this is the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum
nodes.statement_short: The $L_{2k}$ form a finite-type commutative ring spectrum, the initial complex-oriented one.
